report.source_text: She underwent embolisation with access via the left common femoral artery. There was a small distal right superior rectal AVM with filling of a large right rectal haemorrhoid. This was microcanulated to within 1 cm of the fistula point and embolised with 0.1 mL of N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) lipiodol. A flexible sigmoidoscopy a few days later demonstrated no features of recent haemorrhage, and a proctoscopy visualised a moderate sized internal haemorrhoid at 7 o'clock which was banded without complications. She was discharged home the next day.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Pelvic arteriovenous malformation (AVM) presenting with per rectal bleeding
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 17-year-old female with a history of constipation and Implanon use presented to a rural hospital with 2 days of per rectal bleeding (4 episodes) and mild mid-abdominal discomfort. On admission, she was hemodynamically stable with soft abdomen, epigastric and peri-umbilical tenderness, and bright red blood on digital rectal examination. Baseline laboratory investigations showed normal hemoglobin (13 g/dL), normal platelets (247), and normal INR (1.1), indicating no significant anemia or coagulopathy. Computed tomography mesenteric angiogram (CTMA) demonstrated prominent serpiginous vessels in the pelvis surrounding the vagina and involving the anterior aspect of the rectum with right-sided predominance, with arterial phase findings highly suggestive of pelvic AVM and no active gastrointestinal hemorrhage. The patient underwent embolization via left common femoral artery access, where a small distal right superior rectal AVM with filling of a large right rectal hemorrhoid was identified and embolized with N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) lipiodol. Flexible sigmoidoscopy a few days later showed no features of recent hemorrhage, and proctoscopy identified a moderate-sized internal hemorrhoid at 7 o'clock which was banded without complications. She was discharged home the next day.
